scope_note: Both halves: the router as DHCP client, and the router as relay.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Why does the same server answer one VLAN and not the other?

exhibit.content:
VLAN 30                      VLAN 99
    clients ---[ SW-L3 ]------------------------[ DHCP-SRV ]
              10.30.0.1                          10.99.0.10

The DHCP server holds a scope for 10.30.0.0/24. Clients on VLAN 30 send
their requests and receive nothing. A workstation moved onto VLAN 99
obtains an address from the same server immediately.

options.text: A DHCP request is a broadcast and does not leave VLAN 30.
The scope for 10.30.0.0/24 must be defined on the VLAN 30 interface itself.
DHCP works only where the server and the client share an IP subnet by design.
The clients need a static address before they can request a dynamic one.

items.explanation: A client with no address starts by broadcasting, and a broadcast stops at the boundary of its own VLAN, so a server one subnet away never hears it; the workstation moved onto VLAN 99 succeeds because it is then in the same broadcast domain. A relay configured with ip helper-address forwards the request as a unicast. Option B misplaces the scope, which lives on the server. Option C states a limitation that relays exist to remove. Option D reverses the process entirely.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Where does the helper address belong, and what value does it take?

exhibit.content:
! SW-L3 - relevant configuration
!
interface Vlan30
 description client VLAN
 ip address 10.30.0.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface Vlan99
 description server VLAN
 ip address 10.99.0.1 255.255.255.0
!

The DHCP server at 10.99.0.10 must serve clients in VLAN 30.

options.text: On Vlan99, pointing at 10.30.0.1, so replies find their way back.
On Vlan30, pointing at 10.30.0.1, the gateway the clients already use.
On Vlan30, pointing at 10.99.0.10, the address of the DHCP server.
On both interfaces, pointing at 10.99.0.10, so either direction works.

items.explanation: The helper address goes on the interface that receives the clients' broadcasts, which is Vlan30, and names where those requests should be forwarded, which is the server at 10.99.0.10. Option A places it on the server side, where no client broadcast ever arrives. Option B points the relay at the router's own address, creating a loop back to itself. Option D adds a second statement on an interface that has nothing to relay, and would relay the server's own broadcasts back toward the clients.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which command lets R3 accept whatever address the provider offers?

exhibit.content:
! R3 - relevant configuration
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 description circuit to the service provider
 no shutdown
!

The provider issues this circuit's address by DHCP and will not supply a
static allocation. R3 must take whatever address the provider offers,
including the default route that comes with it.

options.text: ip helper-address from the provider's first-hop router
ip dhcp pool WAN followed by a network statement

items.explanation: ip address dhcp puts the interface into client mode, so it requests an address from the provider and installs the default route that accompanies the lease, which is exactly what the circuit requires. Option A configures a relay, which forwards other devices' requests rather than making a request of its own. Option C invents a command; negotiation of this kind is not how IOS expresses it. Option D turns the router into a DHCP server handing out addresses, which is the opposite role.

items.stem: Refer to the exhibit. Which interface obtained its address from a DHCP server?

exhibit.content:
R4# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     198.51.100.37   YES DHCP   up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.4.4.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

options.text: Neither of the two up interfaces

items.explanation: The Method column records how each address arrived, and Gi0/0 reads DHCP while carrying a live address. Option A reads manual, meaning an operator typed the address into the configuration. Option B is unassigned and administratively down, so it has requested nothing. Option C is contradicted by the DHCP entry on Gi0/0, and the Method column exists precisely so this distinction is visible without reading the configuration.
